summary:
NASA FIRMS fire records span two sensors: MODIS (since 2000, with 1 km spatial resolution) and VIIRS (since 2012, with 375 m spatial resolution). Because VIIRS can detect smaller fires, it records approximately 2.4 times as many fire detections as MODIS in South Korea. Simply combining these records makes it appear that fire activity in South Korea increased by 8.2% annually from 2001 to 2025. However, after correcting for sensor differences, the annual trend drops to just 0.6%, indicating almost no change.

We trained a LightGBM model using overlapping MODIS and VIIRS observations from 2012 to 2024 to calibrate VIIRS detections to the MODIS baseline. This allowed us to create a single, continuous fire record spanning November 2000 to November 2026. When tested on years excluded from training, our model reduced prediction error by 33% compared to a rule-based approach.

Using this harmonized dataset, SanBool24 generates verifiable fire history certificates for any region in South Korea, whether selected by administrative district or by drawing a custom area on a map. Carbon credit project managers, insurance claims professionals, and government wildfire officials can use these certificates to make evidence-based decisions grounded in actual changes in fire activity rather than differences between satellite sensors. Each certificate includes a unique 12-character hash that allows anyone to verify its authenticity.
details:
SanBool24 — Project Overview

① Problem

NASA FIRMS fire records span two satellite sensors: MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012).

VIIRS has a smaller pixel size, so it detects many more small fires. In South Korea, VIIRS records about 2.4 times as many fire detections as MODIS.

Simply combining the two datasets creates the false impression that fire activity rose sharply after 2012. In South Korea, the uncorrected annual trend is +8.2%, compared with just +0.6% after calibration.

This distortion can mislead carbon credit risk assessments, insurance claims, and wildfire management budgets.

② Target Users

  • Carbon credit project managers: Verra requires forest carbon projects to provide evidence of historical wildfire frequency and severity. After the 2021 Bootleg Fire in the United States, 1.14 million credits were retired from the buffer pool.
  • Insurance claims professionals: They need reliable evidence that a fire occurred at a specific place and time.
  • Government wildfire officials: They need information on fire seasons, how this year compares with the previous period, and evidence to support budget requests.

③ Solution

Fire detection filtering

  • For finalized historical data, we use the FIRMS type field to keep only presumed vegetation fires (type = 0).
  • Real-time 2026 data has no type field. We fill it using the known locations of persistent heat sources from finalized data, grouped into roughly 1 km grid cells.

Sensor harmonization model

  • Fire detections are aggregated into monthly values on a 0.5° grid.
  • We use LightGBM with monotonic constraints and a Tweedie loss to convert VIIRS observations into MODIS-equivalent detection counts.
  • The training period runs from February 2012 to December 2024. We excluded 2025 because changes in Terra’s orbit caused MODIS to undercount.
  • The most influential features are Fire Radiative Power (FRP, 35%), VIIRS detection counts (27%), and location (15%).
  • Why calibrate VIIRS to MODIS? MODIS is the only continuous record back to 2000. Using it as the reference extends the record without altering earlier observations.

Extending the record with NOAA-20

  • In 2026, S-NPP near-real-time data was interrupted, so we use NOAA-20 instead.
  • Even without retraining, NOAA-20 produced a lower error than S-NPP (118.9 vs. 149.6).

Spatial downscaling for South Korea

  • We distribute each 0.5° cell’s calibrated value among the individual detection points in that cell.
  • This allows calculations for administrative districts (cities, counties) and for custom areas drawn on the map.
  • Correlation with actual MODIS observations is 0.78 at 0.1° and 0.87 at 0.2°. Simple area-based allocation reaches only 0.32 and 0.45.

Fire intensity calibration

  • We calibrated FRP (MW) with the same approach. This reduced error by 39% compared with a simple ratio method.

Account-free report management with hash codes

  • Each issued report receives a unique 12-character hash code.
  • Entering the code in “Find by hash” retrieves the stored original, so users can verify a report and download it again.
  • Design rationale: We removed the login requirement so anyone can use the service immediately. Without accounts there is no personal document storage, so one code handles both retrieval and verification.
  • Report recipients, such as certification bodies, insurers, and budget departments, can also check the original using only the code, without an account.

Final harmonized dataset

  • One continuous fire record from November 2000 to November 2026: 5,384,508 grid-month records.
    • 2000–2002: Terra-corrected observations
    • 2002–2024: direct MODIS observations
    • 2025 onward: VIIRS converted to the MODIS baseline, with uncertainty intervals

④ Validation

Model performance

  • We held out each year from 2020 to 2024, trained on the preceding years, and tested on the held-out year.
  • Our model’s error was 33% lower than the best rule-based baseline (149.6 vs. 221.1).
  • It beat the baseline in all five test years, with an overall bias of −0.3%.

Uncertainty calibration

  • The nominal 80% prediction intervals achieved 81.4% empirical coverage.

Fire activity index

  • Our five-level index, which compares fire activity against historical norms, achieved 67% category agreement. Simply combining sensor-specific indices achieved 52%.

Long-term trend in South Korea

  • Before calibration: +8.2% per year
  • After calibration: +0.6% per year
  • Much of the apparent increase comes from the difference in sensor capability, not from a change in fire activity.

⑤ Implemented Service Features

  • Immediate access with no login or registration
  • Select an administrative area (province, city/county/district) or draw a custom area on the map
  • 12 data items: fire observation summary, fire observation locations, monthly observation trend, observation confidence, annual fire trend, large-fire frequency, high-risk season, nearest fire, fire intensity classes, day/night comparison, previous-period comparison, fire hotspots
  • Report preview and PDF download in Korean or English
  • A unique 12-character hash code for every issued report
  • “Find by hash” for verification and re-download
  • A 25-year wildfire timelapse on the homepage
  • Sentinel-2 satellite map

⑥ Expected Impact

  • Carbon credit projects: Evidence-based wildfire risk assessment from a consistent record back to 2000.
  • Insurance claims: One report containing evidence of fire observations at a specific place and time.
  • Local governments: Wildfire budgets planned around observed fire seasons and long-term patterns.
  • Verifiable reports: Recipients can retrieve the stored original with its 12-character code and compare it with the copy they received.
  • Why this matters now: The problem already exists. Since 2025, changes in Terra’s orbit have caused MODIS to undercount by about 9%, so our system already uses VIIRS-calibrated MODIS-equivalent values from 2025 onward.

⑦ Limitations and Next Steps

Current limitations

  • Calibrated values are distributed to detection points, but MODIS geolocation uncertainty of about 1–5 km means areas smaller than about 5 km are not meaningful. The system cannot support parcel-level decisions.
  • The data measures fire detection counts, not burned area.
  • Because there are no accounts, a lost code means a previously issued report cannot be retrieved.

Future development

  • Global expansion: The harmonization model is already trained on global 0.5° data.
  • Pilot programs: Work with carbon credit projects and local governments to test the platform in practice.
  • Burned area integration: Add burned-area data for a fuller picture of wildfire impact.

⑧ Technology Stack

  • Data processing and machine learning: Python, DuckDB, pandas, LightGBM, pytest
  • Backend: Java 21, Spring Boot 4.1, JPA, MyBatis, PostgreSQL 17 + PostGIS 3.5, Flyway, Docker Compose, AWS S3 (issued report storage)
  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, TanStack Query, i18next (Korean/English), jsPDF, html2canvas
  • Deployment: Cloudflare Workers (frontend), AWS EC2 with GitHub Actions (backend)
